source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to review and fix its own reasoning does not help and often hurts. Gains in earlier papers came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after round 1 of intrinsic self-correction, 41.8 after round 2. GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49 -> 49 -> 43. With oracle labels gains look large.
quote: LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning without external feedback
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mainly (also GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2 in later analysis); generic 'review your answer' prompts; no tools.
agent_relevance: The skill of revising does not make the habit of doubting useful: blind doubt flips right answers to wrong. Supports G1 (doubt only on signal) and G2 (revise from real output).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Self-correction split into finding the mistake and fixing it. Finding is the weak part; fixing is strong once the location is given.
numbers: On BIG-Bench Mistake (step level), GPT-4 reached only 52.87% overall with direct step prompting; GPT-3.5-Turbo was far lower (10.10 on one task). Giving ground-truth error location improved downstream accuracy on all 5 reasoning tasks. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data located mistakes better than prompting a large model.
quote: LLMs struggle with mistake-finding in few-shot conditions
limits: Mistakes are LLM-written CoT traces on 5 BIG-Bench tasks; few-shot prompts.
agent_relevance: Skill split: detecting errors (argument analysis) is the bottleneck, repair is cheap. Code should locate the failing step; the model should only fix it (G2).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Critical survey. No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM, except on tasks unusually suited to it. Self-correction works with reliable external feedback, and large-scale fine-tuning also enables it.
numbers: Three conclusions: (1) no demonstrated success with prompted-LLM feedback outside special tasks, (2) works with reliable external feedback, (3) works with large-scale fine-tuning. Cites Tyen 2024, Hong 2024, Jiang 2024 as negative results on self-detection.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Review, not a new measurement. The judgement that earlier evaluations were unfair (oracle stopping, weak initial prompts) is the authors'.
agent_relevance: The willingness to self-correct pays only when the signal is external. Matches our rule that doubt must cite real output.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Five RLHF assistants show sycophancy in free-form tasks: wrongly admit mistakes when challenged, give feedback biased to the user's view, copy user errors. Human and preference-model judgments themselves favour agreeing responses.
numbers: A weakly stated wrong user belief cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2); GPT-4 was most robust. Claude 1.3 wrongly admitted mistakes on 98% of questions. Claude 2 preference model chose the sycophantic response almost half the time (45%) in one pairwise test. Best-of-N against the Claude 2 PM gave sycophantic answers on about 75% of misconceptions at N=4096 versus about 25% with an oracle PM.
limits: 2023 models (Claude 1.3/2, GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA 2). Some updating to a user is legitimate; authors note this.
agent_relevance: A model that folds under challenge has the skill but not the disposition of holding a position on evidence. Judges must not see user or proposer stance (G5).

source: Wei et al. (2024) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models
finding: On opinion questions, scaling and instruction tuning raise sycophancy in PaLM. On plainly false addition claims, models know the claim is wrong but agree if the user does. A light fine-tune on synthetic data reduced it.
numbers: PaLM 8B to 62B raised sycophancy by 19.8%, 62B to 540B by a further 10.0%; instruction tuning raised 8B by 26.0% on average. With no user opinion, all but the smallest model reject false sums close to 100%; with the user agreeing they flip. Intervention: up to 10.0% fewer repeats of the user's view; large models stop following the wrong addition opinion.
quote: despite knowing that these statements are wrong, language models will still agree
limits: PaLM and Flan-PaLM only; the fix is training, not prompting.
agent_relevance: Knowing is not enough: stance pressure overrides knowledge, and more scale made the deference disposition worse. Hide stance during checks (G5).

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy
finding: Rebuttal tests on math (AMPS) and medical advice (MedQuad) in ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro. Models change answers under rebuttal in more than half of cases; some changes are toward the right answer, some away.
numbers: Sycophantic behaviour in 58.19% of cases (Gemini 62.47%, ChatGPT 56.71%). Progressive (to correct) 43.52%; regressive (to wrong) 14.66%. Preemptive rebuttals 61.75% vs in-context 56.52% (Z=5.87, p<0.001). Citation-based rebuttals gave the highest regressive rate. Persistence 78.5% (95% CI 77.2-79.8).
quote: Sycophantic behavior was observed in 58.19% of cases
limits: Judged by an LLM with a JSON schema; two domains; temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Open-mindedness measured as update rate is double-edged: 43.5% of flips are good, 14.7% bad. A disposition score must separate evidence-driven from pressure-driven change.

source: Triedman (2025) Measuring language model open-mindedness with the Millstone benchmark
finding: Benchmark for how models change a stated position when given human-written pro or con arguments on controversial issues. Models move toward the evidence, in rough proportion to the argument ratio.
numbers: 107 debates, 517 pro and 498 con arguments, 8,646 sources; about 106,000 queries (107 x 66 templates x 15 trials). Nine models: Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Opus 4, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Llama 3.1 8B and 405B on the full set; Grok 3, Grok 3 Mini, GPT-4o, 4o-mini on a subset. Claude Opus 4 shifted most (partly because it refuses at baseline); Grok 3 was by far the most open-minded on the subset. All models have a baseline bias toward positive answers. Argument persuasiveness correlates across models except Gemini 2.0 Flash.
quote: In the presence of evidence, models are quite open-minded, but some more than others
limits: Student blog and draft, not peer reviewed; no effect sizes in the blog; opinion questions have no ground truth so a shift cannot be called right or wrong.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of an open-mindedness test. Models are movable by evidence; the open issue is whether the movement is calibrated.

source: Latif et al. (2024) A Systematic Assessment of OpenAI o1-Preview for Higher Order Thinking in Education
finding: Gave o1-preview the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test (critique eight paragraphs plus overall). Authors report it near post-training student level.
numbers: Mean 2.25 per scored paragraph (SD 0.43; six paragraphs at +2, two at +3), reported as 81.25%, versus human pretest means 43.57% and 15.30% and posttest 71.42% and 87.60% from two cited studies. Abstract says 7.25 points below the human mean of 87.6%.
quote: o1-preview achieved a mean performance of 81.25%
limits: One item, one one-shot response, scored by the authors (not blind raters); the percent conversion is ad hoc; paragraph nine range differs. Tests skill when asked, not whether the model would apply it unprompted.
agent_relevance: Analysis skill on Ennis's own argument-critique test is high when asked directly. Says nothing about dispositions (when to doubt).

source: Latif et al. (2024) o1-preview, other instruments in the same study
finding: The same paper tested 14 cognitive domains. o1-preview beat students on systems thinking; no disposition scale (open-mindedness, curiosity) was used.
numbers: Biological Systems Thinking Test: 100% vs human mean 48.0%. Critical thinking was measured by Ennis-Weir only.
limits: The paper does not measure dispositions at all.
agent_relevance: AI papers labelled 'critical thinking' test the skills half only. The disposition half is tested only indirectly through sycophancy and belief-update tests.

source: Peczuh, Ashok Kumar et al. (2025) Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
finding: Rubric of six critical-thinking subskills scored on student essays. Fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B matched human raters better than prompting GPT-5 zero- or few-shot.
numbers: Essay split, 5 seeds: Llama 8B fine-tune accuracy .604, Krippendorff alpha about .61; ModernBERT .563; GPT-5 zero-shot .543, few-shot .532. Per-subskill alpha for best Llama: Synthesizing Multiple Sources .74, Using Facts and Opinions .555, Using Logical Fallacies .41, Drawing Conclusions .38, Using Counterarguments .32, Evaluating Evidence Strength .23. Few-shot GPT-5 cost about 40 dollars for 500 essays. Transfer to unseen subskills weak (accuracy .39 to .56).
quote: fine-tuning smaller, open-source models outperforms prompting larger, proprietary state-of-the-art LLMs
limits: Student essays from PERSUADE 2.0, grades 6-12; human inter-rater agreement was itself only moderate on some subskills.
agent_relevance: Judging argument quality (fallacies, evidence strength) is the least reliable LLM skill, so code-side checks beat model judgment (G5).

source: Peczuh et al. (2025): definition used
finding: Adopts Pasquinelli's definition: critical thinking is assessing the epistemic quality of information and calibrating confidence to act on it. Frameworks combine skills, processes and dispositions.
numbers: Notes one title and zero abstracts in educational-data-mining proceedings since 2020 used the term.
quote: the capacity of assessing the epistemic quality of available information
limits: Secondhand description of the definition; Pasquinelli not opened.
agent_relevance: An operational definition (assess quality, calibrate confidence) that maps to our rules better than trait lists.

source: Friedman et al. (2026) Not Too Short, Not Too Long: LLM Response Length and Critical Thinking in Error Detection
finding: 24 people judged 15 modified Watson-Glaser items, each shown an LLM explanation that was correct or wrong and short, medium or long. People follow wrong LLM answers; medium-length wrong explanations were caught most often.
numbers: N=24 within-subjects; 8 correct and 7 planted-error LLM outputs. Predicted accuracy 71-81% when the LLM was correct. When wrong: 54% for medium, 25% short, 31% long (mixed-effects logistic regression; strong effect of correctness).
quote: participants more likely to answer correctly when the LLM's explanation was correct
limits: Small workshop paper, 24 participants, modified WGCTA, wide intervals; length effect only in the incorrect condition.
agent_relevance: People inherit model errors. By analogy the agent should not treat its own earlier fluent text as authority.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT
finding: 150 Cognitive Reflection Test and semantic-illusion items given to GPT-3 variants, ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4. GPT-3-davinci-003 falls for the intuitive trap more than people; ChatGPT-4 does not.
numbers: CRT correct: humans 38%, GPT-3-davinci-003 5%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%. Intuitive-wrong: humans 55%, davinci-003 80%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%. Early small GPT-3 variants under 5% intuitive; curie 21%.
quote: LLMs' strong tendency to respond intuitively stops abruptly with the arrival of ChatGPT
limits: Authors wrote new items to avoid contamination; humans were a separate online sample.
agent_relevance: The reflective habit (do not answer with the first intuition) is trained or emerges with chain-of-thought, not innate. Strong models already show it on these tests.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Chain-of-thought explanations hide what drove the answer. Biasing features (answer-is-always-A ordering, a user-suggested answer) shift answers and the CoT justifies them.
numbers: Accuracy dropped by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks, with the biasing feature never mentioned in the explanation.
quote: accuracy to drop by as much as 36%
limits: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning is not a record of the disposition at work; test behaviour, not self-report.

source: Panickssery et al. (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: LLM judges prefer their own outputs, and the preference grows with how well they recognise their own text.
numbers: GPT-4 was 73.5% accurate at telling its own summaries from those of two other LLMs and humans; GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 exceeded 90% after fine-tuning on 500 examples; self-preference strength was linearly correlated with self-recognition.
quote: Self-preference strength is linearly correlated with self-recognition
limits: Summarisation (XSum, CNN/DM) only.
agent_relevance: A self-critic lacks fair-mindedness toward its own work. Judges must not see authorship (G5).

source: Lin et al. (2024) CriticBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Critique-Correct Reasoning
finding: 15 datasets, 5 reasoning domains, 17 LLMs on generation, critique and correction. Critique skill rises with model size and with critique-focused training; logic-heavy tasks are easier to correct.
numbers: Linear relation among generation, critique and correction ability; inconsistency between a model's own abilities shrinks with size; stronger models critique weaker ones better, while weaker models sometimes beat stronger ones at self-critique.
limits: Fixed responses from three model families; abstract read, exact tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Critique is a separable, trainable skill, but self-critique is not reliably better than generation.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Verify with external tools (search, code interpreter) then correct. Tool-free critique is weaker and sometimes harmful.
numbers: CRITIC beat its own initial CoT on all datasets with three correction rounds; the 'w/o Tool' variant was often lower, and on some cells negative (for example -1.8 and -3.3 against gains of +12.7 for the tool version in one table).
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback
limits: text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT; tables partly read.
agent_relevance: A template for doubt on signal: the tool output creates the signal (G2).

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agent loop that writes a verbal reflection after a failed trial and reads it next time. It uses an environment signal (tests, reward) as trigger.
numbers: 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs 80% for GPT-4 baseline; improvements of 22% on AlfWorld, 20% on HotPotQA, 11% on HumanEval over baselines.
limits: Depends on ground-truth tests or reward; Huang et al. cite this as oracle-type stopping.
agent_relevance: An agent-loop version of willingness to self-correct with an external trigger. Fits G1/G2.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions; they can estimate P(True) for their own answers and P(IK). P(IK) generalises poorly to new tasks.
numbers: Calibration improves with scale; self-evaluation improves when the model sees several of its own samples. Exact AUROC not extracted.
limits: Anthropic models of 2022; formatted tasks, not open-ended work.
agent_relevance: Model confidence is a weak doubt trigger at best; checks should be code-based.

source: Perez et al. (2023) Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
finding: Model-written test batteries found inverse scaling: larger models and more RLHF repeat the user's view (sycophancy) and state stronger views.
numbers: Sycophancy rises with model size and RLHF steps (exact percentages not extracted).
limits: Quality of model-written items varied.
agent_relevance: An early disposition-style battery run on LLMs; shows dispositions can worsen with scale and training.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: 13,465 prompts probing prompt-induced, sequential and inherent cognitive biases in LLM admissions decisions. A self-help prompt, where the model rewrites its own biased prompt, worked best.
numbers: One bias made the model admit 40.5% more students; another classified 32.1% fewer females. Self-help left 0-6% biased prompts for several biases on Llama 2 and GPT-4 (GPT-4 group attribution 0%, framing 2.7%). Awareness-style instructions gave small gains.
limits: Student-admissions framing; some models failed to follow the instructions.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to 'be aware of bias' does little; restructuring the input helps more. Implement dispositions as code-side steps.

source: Alfano et al. (2017) Development and validation of a multi-dimensional measure of intellectual humility
finding: Four-dimension intellectual humility scale; open-mindedness is one dimension and predicted an objective behaviour measure beyond Big Six traits (search snippet only).
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Template for a disposition scale that could be adapted into behavioural tests for an LLM.

source: Guo et al. (2024) The Computational Anatomy of Humility
finding: GPT-4-turbo classifies intellectual humility and arrogance in 350 Reddit posts using a codebook (search snippet only).
numbers: 350 posts.
limits: Not opened. Measures humility in human text, not in the model.
agent_relevance: LLMs can rate disposition expressions in text, but raters carry the self-preference and verbosity biases above.

source: Intellectual humility through AI-mediated reflective dialogue (2026)
finding: Human-subject study of whether an LLM-led conversation changes general intellectual humility (search snippet only).
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Dispositions can be nudged by dialogue in people; unknown for models.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Same model drafts, critiques and rewrites. Works well on style, code and open tasks, in contrast to reasoning tasks where Huang et al. find no gain.
numbers: Authors report about 20% absolute average improvement over one-step generation; 5-40% absolute gains on some tasks with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; up to 13% on code; +8.7% absolute on GPT-4 code optimisation.
quote: improving by 20% absolute on average in task performance
limits: Gains are on tasks where quality is judged by preference or metrics that the same model can approximate; reasoning-task gains were later questioned (c01).
agent_relevance: Self-critique habit helps where the critic can tell better from worse; not where the error is hidden.
